title: Praggnanandhaa Jumps From Last To 1st With Hat Trick
summary: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu started at the bottom, but now he's at the top of Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown 2026 with a 1.5-point lead after day two. He pulled a hat trick with two wins against GM Hikaru Nakamura and one against GM Fabiano Caruana. GM Javokhir Sindarov and Caruana are tied in second on 8.5 points, while Nakamura—who started the day in first—is in last with 8. Day three, featuring rounds seven through nine, is on Thursday, October 29, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 18:00 CET / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings Praggnanandhaa has scored the biggest bonus so far with $9,000 for his wins in the tournament. All the draws are added to the winner's pot at the end, and so far $19,000 is the size of that contribution. Praggnanandhaa accepted the result, but he wasn't happy with the quality of his play. Comparing his performance to the previous day, he said, "I think today was also bad, but I was more lucky today." Referencing his first win against Nakamura, he said, "I was just lucky, and obviously that kind of carried through the day." He quipped: "There were some bad games, there were some okay games, but okay, whatever, if I'm winning then it's fine. I'll take it." Praggnanandhaa made just one draw in six games, winning four and losing one. He started by winning the first game of the mini-match with Sindarov when, in an equal but complicated heavy-piece endgame, Sindarov failed to find the only path.

title: Oro, Taher Lead 9z Globant To Victory In October Chess Club Showdown
summary: For the second month in a row, 9z Globant won the Chess Club Showdown on October 28, once again defeating Team Liquid in the finals. They were the two highest-scoring teams after a two-hour arena of five-minute blitz games. In the finals, 50 players from each of the top two teams played head-to-head two-game matches in rating order to crown a champion. GM Faustino Oro, the highest-rated player on 9z Globant, led them to a convincing victory with a 1.5-0.5 win over GM Christopher Yoo. 9z Globant flexed their strength throughout the day, winning the arena and the finals. They had 10 competitors with blitz ratings over 3000, and their whole 50-player team in the finals held ratings over 2000. That meant that they had rating advantages on every board throughout the finals, leading to a dominant 79-21 victory. Chess Club Showdowns are unique events where super GMs like Vincent Keymer, Gata Kamsky, and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave compete in the same event as amateurs. Many of the 6,400 participants got to play against titled opponents, some for the very first time. GM Magnus Carlsen had to withdraw at the last minute, while other top Team Liquid players, GMs Fabiano Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, were unavailable because they were competing in the Clutch Chess Champions Showdown. Even without Carlsen, Caruana, and Praggnanandhaa, Team Liquid finished second, closer to 9z Globant than to third-place Team Vitality. Vitality, FUT Esports, and Natus Vincere rounded out the top five team scores, all taking home prizes. In a field stacked with strong GMs, Chinese teenage FM Ziyuan Xu managed to win individual first place in the arena section with 82 points. He scored numerous upsets throughout the event, including this impressive game against GM Matthias Bluebaum, who finished in fourth place.

title: Sipke Ernst - Attacking Chess: Know When to Strike
summary:
GM Sipke Ernst explains how to recognize when an attack is truly justified, focusing on factors such as development, king safety, open lines and central control. Through successful and failed examples, he shows when to strike, when to build pressure, and when a quieter or prophylactic move is the stronger choice.

Attacking Chess: Know When to Strike

by Sipke Ernst

Most players know how to attack. What separates strong players from the rest is knowing when. In this course, GM Sipke Ernst, a grandmaster from the Netherlands and experienced coach, addresses the mistake he sees most often in his own students: attacking with the right idea, at the wrong moment.

Free video sample: Introduction

Free video sample: Example Game: Ernst - Mediema

You'll learn to read the signals that indicate an attack is justified, such as a shortage of defenders around the enemy king, a lead in development, or open lines and weaknesses near the king's position. Just as important, you'll study examples of attacks that failed, and why.

The course also covers when to increase pressure gradually instead of forcing complications, when a prophylactic move does more for your attack than another aggressive one, and how central control determines whether a flank attack succeeds or backfires. A final chapter draws on GM Sipke Ernst's own games to show how strong grandmasters generate attacking chances even from inferior positions.

What you'll get:

A practical framework for recognizing when to attack, and when to hold back

Instructive examples of both successful and flawed attacking play

Chapters on pressure vs. calculation, prophylaxis, flank attacks, and attacking from worse positions

Real games from GM Sipke Ernst's own practice

Learn to attack when it counts, not just when you want to.

Running time: 5 hours 18 minutes

title: KazChess Masters: Mamedov and Makhnev set the pace in Almaty
summary:
Kazakh grandmasters Edgar Mamedov (pictured) and Denis Makhnev share the lead at the KazChess Masters in Almaty after three rounds, both with 2½ points. Mamedov, aged 16, started with two consecutive wins, while Makhnev caught up by defeating Aram Hakobyan in round three. Three of the five international participants - Daniil Dubov, Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Denis Lazavik - are half a point behind the leading duo. | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Kazakh duo in the lead

Kazakhstan's Edgar Mamedov and Denis Makhnev are sharing the lead at the KazChess Masters in Almaty after three rounds of play. Both have collected 2½ points, with Makhnev joining his compatriot at the top of the standings thanks to a third-round victory over Aram Hakobyan. Three of the five international participants - Daniil Dubov, Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Denis Lazavik - are half a point behind the leaders.

The KazChess Masters is a ten-player round-robin tournament taking place in Almaty, Kazakhstan, from 26 October to 3 November. The field features five local representatives (rated 2451 to 2581) and five foreign grandmasters, all of whom are rated above 2600. Among the visitors are Russian GM Daniil Dubov, Uzbek GM Shamsiddin Vokhidov, Armenian GM Aram Hakobyan and Belarusian GM Denis Lazavik, while Azerbaijan's GM Mahammad Muradli entered as the top seed.

The opening round saw four decisive games, all won by white. Dubov defeated 14-year-old Mark Smirnov, Lazavik got the better of Muradli, and the Kazakh duo of Edgar Mamedov and Denis Makhnev scored wins over Sauat Nurgaliyev and Alua Nurman, respectively.

Lazavik v. Muradli

Annotations by Stefan Liebig

Lazavik, who reached the final of the Esports World Cup a few weeks ago but lost to Magnus Carlsen, defeated the tournament's top seed. The 19-year-old online specialist from Minsk showed that he is also a force to be reckoned with over the board. Against the Azerbaijani GM, he gained the initiative out of a Sicilian Defence.

After a few less-than-accurate moves, a position arose which, despite the material imbalance, was assessed as equal by the engine. Muradli then embarked on a risky pawn hunt with 28...Be5?? . Lazavik responded with 29.c4?! – also not optimal, but the position was already noticeably better for White:

The 2015 U12 world champion stuck to his (mistaken) plan and captured on g3: 29...Bxg3??+- . There followed 30.Bc3! Re6? 31.Qg5 Bc7 32.Rd7 , and Black resigned in a hopeless position that had quickly turned around.

The threats of Rxc7 followed by Qd8+, as well as mate with the queen and bishop on the long diagonal, cannot be stopped.

Denis Lazavik | Photo: Lennart Ootes

Mamedov, aged 16 and the lowest-rated grandmaster in the field, became the sole leader in round two by defeating Hakobyan with the black pieces. The game lasted 92 moves and gave the youngster a perfect 2/2 score. Meanwhile, Vokhidov defeated Muradli, handing the top seed his second consecutive loss.

Smirnov bounced back from his opening defeat by beating Nurman.

Smirnov v. Nurman

Annotations by Stefan Liebig

Out of a King's Indian Defence reached by transposition, Smirnov quickly obtained the better position. Nurman defended well, however, equalised and reached the position above: White is more active, but Black's counterplay keeps the advantage within limits.

Black should have attacked the excellent white knight here with 29...Ba6. Instead, with both players in time trouble, the two-time Olympiad silver medallist went pawn-hunting: 29...Rxa2?? 30.Rxe8 Qxe8 31.Re1 Qf8 32.Qxd3 Ra7 33.Nb6 (even stronger would have been 33.Qb3). 33...Ba6 Too late! 34.Qc3 Qd8?!+- .

A pointless attack on the knight. White simply plays 35.Re6! , and the knight is untouchable anyway because of the mating attack with queen and rook against the now exposed king. Nurman defended the g-pawn with 35...Rg7 . But the position was already hopeless, and Smirnov converted his advantage confidently.

14-year-old Kazakh talent Mark Smirnov | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Wednesday's third round produced considerably fewer decisive results. Four of the five encounters ended drawn, while Makhnev defeated Hakobyan with the white pieces to join Mamedov in the lead. The 25-year-old Kazakh GM has now won both his games with white.

Mamedov, meanwhile, drew his game against Muradli to remain undefeated on 2½/3.

With six rounds still to play, the two Kazakh leaders have made the most of the opening stage of the tournament. Mamedov has recorded two wins and a draw, while Makhnev has followed the same pattern, with his victories coming in both games in which he had the white pieces.

title: Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown - Live!
summary:
Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown is a high-profile rapid tournament gathering four elite competitors. Javokhir Sindarov, who is set to challenge Gukesh Dommaraju for the World Championship title next month, joins Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu in a three-day battle. The competition runs from 27 to 29 October and follows a "clutch" structure of three double round-robins, where results become progressively more valuable with each round-robin. | Follow the action live starting at 18.00 CET (13.00 ET, 22.30 IST) | Photo: Crystal Fuller

Day 2

The event follows a "clutch" structure of three double round-robins, with two games per pairing in each stage for a total of 18 games per player. The time control is 10 minutes for the entire game, plus a 5-second increment per move. An anti-early-draw regulation is in effect: draws are not permitted before Black's 60 th move.

The innovation lies in the escalating scoring system, as results become progressively more valuable with each round-robin.

Round-robin one: Players earn 1 point for a win, ½ for a draw, and 0 for a loss

Round-robin two: Players earn 2 points for a win, 1 for a draw, and 0 for a loss

Round-robin three: Players earn 3 points for a win, 1 for a draw, and 0 for a loss

title: Dragons of the Olympiad 2026 - The Monthly Dragon
summary:
In this Olympiad special of the Monthly Dragon, Chris Ward looks at five Dragon games from a wide range of rating levels and shows just how successful the opening was in Samarkand. The examples highlight typical Dragon themes such as pressure on the c file, the strength of the dark squared bishop, exchange sacrifices, tactical ideas around the queenside and the importance of knowing the right plans once the opening theory ends. Chris also examines several instructive mistakes, showing how quickly a position can collapse when White loses track of key Dragon motifs. | Photo: John Upham

The Monthly Dragon

with GM Chris Ward

The British Grandmaster Chris Ward is always delighted if he can play his favourite opening as Black: the Sicilian Dragon.

Ward's knowledge about this strong opening is covered in several of his books , his blog on chesspublishing and his three, greatly popular FritzTrainers in our ChessBase shop .

With the new ChessBase series "The Monthly Dragon", the passionate Salsa dancer is showing us the newest tactics, plans and development of this fascinating opening.

Lucky for us, the dragon is an opening, played by some of the best players in the world. This means, Chris probably won't run out of fuel for new content.
